 Michael J. Fox Admits He Thought People Would ‘Crucify’ Him for Joking About Parkinson’s Diagnosis in “Curb Your Enthusiasm”
 In the end, Fox said that “people really loved” the episode
 People Follow Meredith Wilshere Add to Preferred Sources Sun, November 8, 2026 at 9:59 PM UTC Michael J. Fox and Larry David on 'Curb Your Enthusiasm'
Credit: Hbo/Kobal/Shutterstock NEED TO KNOW
 Michael J. Fox feared viewers would criticize his 2011 cameo with Larry David on Curb Your Enthusiasm before agreeing to the role
 Fox said improvising as himself made the HBO comedy experience especially fun
 The actor called the episode a breakthrough for changing perceptions of people living with Parkinson's
 Michael J. Fox initially thought he would get "crucified" for his appearance on Curb Your Enthusiasm with Larry David.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement While talking to Michael Sebastian for an interview with Esquire , Fox, 65, recalled how much fun he had filming his 2011 cameo on the series . Sebastian started the conversation by mentioning that Fox was "in one of my favorite episodes of Curb Your Enthusiasm where you play Larry's upstairs neighbor and he accuses you of using your Parkinson's to basically get sympathy and so on and ruin his life."
 When the journalist questioned why he decided to do the episode in the first place, Fox replied, "Oh, because it's hilarious."
 "Larry called me up and said he had this idea and I said, 'No, they'll crucify us. They're gonna kill us if we do this.' I said that. And he said, 'Oh, okay, well,' I said, 'No, that's not a problem. That recommends it to me.' And it was just a great time," Fox shared. 
 Larry David and Michael J. Fox on 'Curb Your Enthusiasm' 
 "It's pure improv, except they have the central theme and they lay it out and you pick up on that and you just run it. And I played myself so I can't screw it up," Fox recalled.
 Advertisement Advertisement Fox joined season 8 of the HBO sitcom to play himself as David's upstairs neighbor. A fictional version of David believes Fox is going out of his way to ruin his life, wearing heavy boots and stomping around upstairs and shaking sodas before handing them to David.
 Despite initial nerves, Fox said that "people really loved it."
 "It was a big breakthrough again in this Parkinson's point of view, bringing people into our way of thinking, which was we're people in society, and we have to reach out for what we need, and we have to express ourselves," Fox shared. "So great. He was just so cool and so funny. He would do things that I didn't expect."
 Diagnosed with early-onset Parkinson's in 1991, Fox kept his diagnosis private before publicly sharing the news in 1998.
 Advertisement Advertisement His time on Curb Your Enthusiasm includes a moment from Fox's real life, where the late Rush Limbaugh was convinced that the actor went out of his way to shake a soda before handing it to him.
 "In what world do you manufacture a major neurological disease that's systemic and paralyzing and debilitating? I make that up to make Rush Limbaugh's day a little worse? It's crazy," he joked.
 More to explore
 Fox shared that "it was really good because it taught me to fight for what I believed in. It was very simple."
 "I was just saying research freedom," he added.
